Hey everyone, I'm ACatNight.

I've posted a few things here about learning, side projects, and programming, but I realized I never really introduced myself.

So yeah, I guess I'll do that now.

I'm a software engineering student from China. I started programming with Minecraft server development, and later I started making my own plugins and working on different projects.

One of my main open-source projects is WorldScript, a Minecraft RPG region and event framework.

During my second semester, I spent most of my time working at a small startup that had just started not long before.

It was probably one of the most different experiences I've had so far.

I worked on real projects, fixed real bugs, and had to deal with things that I never really had to deal with at school.

I also made a mistake at work, and I was eventually let go because of it.

That honestly sucked.

But looking back, I still got a lot out of that experience. I learned a lot from actually working on projects, and it changed how I think about software development.

Before that, I mostly thought being a developer was just about writing code and making things work.

After working on real projects, I realized there was a lot more to it.

You have to think about how things are designed, how to find problems, how to work with other people, how to deal with deadlines, and what to do when something goes wrong.

It also made me think more about what I actually want to do in the future.

After the semester, I came back to school and started working on my own projects again.

Right now, I'm mainly learning:

  • C#
  • .NET backend development
  • AI applications

I'm also working with things like ASP.NET Core, databases, Redis, RabbitMQ, Docker, Linux, and async programming.

I'm also rebuilding my main side project, StudyTree.

It's an AI learning reflection project built around a simple question:

What do I actually know, what am I missing, and what should I learn next?

I still have a lot to learn, but for now, I just like building things, breaking them, fixing them, and seeing where it goes.

That's pretty much where I am right now.

Nice to meet you.

articles.title: I Optimized My Bump Version Tool and Made It 1,000,000x Faster Than Its Python Counterparts.
articles.description: Hello again, fellow Rustaceans, Pythonistas in denial, and the three people on earth who genuinely...
articles.body_html:
Hello again, fellow Rustaceans, Pythonistas in denial, and the three people on earth who genuinely enjoy reading version bumper release notes 👋!

If you were here for my last post, where I rewrote bump2version in Rust and declared it ~10,000x faster than the Python CLI, you may recall that I ended it with a vague threat about future benchmarks. The Mossad agents who consulted on the architecture wrote "this is not over" in the margin of their whiteboard. I ignored it.

I should have listened.

Because in the weeks since that post, I went back in. Deep in. I committed crimes against cargo build that will haunt me during thunderstorms. I --release'd things that should not be --release'd. I made Claude hallucinate a performance chart at 3AM and then used it to motivate myself.

The result: bump2version 0.2.1.

Now 1,000,000× faster than its Python counterparts. Yes, I am counting subprocess overhead.

The Soviet material resurfaced. It always does.

Let's get into it.

🤔 Wait, We Already Did This. Why Are We Here Again?

Because 0.2.0 shipped, and I immediately opened my Gmail inbox.

The audacity of the open-source community. The audacity, bro! I build something 10,000x faster and within days there are requests. "Can it watch files?", "Can it detect which manifests I'm using?", "Can I run it in the browser?", "Can I use it with Go?", "Can I use it with Java?", "Can my Ruby project use it?". I ain't got no time for this. I need to take a little break and play CS2 with the boys!

I looked at these emails. I looked at the ceiling. I looked at my coffee. The coffee looked back at me with the hollow expression of a language runtime that has seen too many package manager debates.

And then I cracked my knuckles and got to work.

🕵️ The Mossad Agents Return

I thought I was done with the Mossad agents after 0.2.0. I was not.

They came back. Same 3AM knock. Same whiteboard. But this time they brought slides. Twelve of them. With bullet points. And speaker notes. One slide was just the word "BRANCHLESS" in 72-point font with a red circle around it.

Their new requirements:

  1. memchr for all hot-path string scanning. "You are doing .contains() in a loop like an animal", they said. I was.
  2. SmallVec for version component storage. Because heap-allocating a Vec<u8> for three numbers (major, minor, patch) is an insult to modern CPU cache lines.
  3. Branchless arithmetic for the bump itself. No if major { ... } else if minor { ... } nonsense. One lookup table. One store. Done.
  4. Watch mode. They wanted to know the moment a file changed. I asked why. They said that was classified.
  5. Auto-detect language manifests. "You scan Cargo.toml like it's the only file in the world", they observed, correctly. "What about pyproject.toml? pom.xml? go.mod? Are Go developers not also suffering?"

They are. They are very much also suffering.

I implemented every point. The Mossad agents reviewed the diff, said "passable", and vanished into the root filesystem like a well-placed .gitignore entry.

⚡ The 1,000,000× Number

Let me be absolutely scientifically honest with you for one sentence before I stop being honest: the 1,000,000× number compares the full bump-my-version CLI round-trip (importing Python, loading dependencies, spawning a subprocess) against our in-process library call with a warm cache and a SmallVec.

One is a sports car. The other is a person who has to call a taxi, wait 12 minutes, and explain where they're going in a language they only partially speak.

Now let's look at the real numbers.

🔥 New Benchmarks: 0.2.0 vs 0.2.1 vs Python

Operation bump2version 0.2.0 bump2version 0.2.1 Python pyO3 FFI bump-my-version CLI
Parse + bump + serialize ~57 µs ~0.4 µs ~79 µs ~585 ms
File search/replace (1k lines) ~65 µs ~11 µs ~1.7 µs ~590 ms
File search/replace (100k lines) ~4.2 ms ~0.9 ms N/A ~600 ms
Config file parse ~800 µs ~140 µs N/A ~500 ms (on import)

Versus the Python CLI subprocess: ((500 x 1000) ÷ 0.4) = ~1,250,000× faster for a version parse-bump-serialize. We round down to 1,000,000x for humility. The Mossad agents said rounding up was acceptable. We preferred honesty.

What got fast and why:

  • memchr replaced every inner-loop string search. memchr is basically SIMD-accelerated strchr and it is unreasonably good at its one job.
  • SmallVec<[VersionPart; 8]> means version component vectors never touch the allocator for reasonable semver (≤8 parts). Stack-allocated. L1 cache. Zero malloc.
  • Branchless bump arithmetic: the bump logic is now a lookup into a const table of which component to increment and which to zero. The CPU's branch predictor doesn't even have to sweat.
  • Arc<Regex> cache from 0.2.0 was kept. The regex is compiled exactly once and shared. The Mossad agents reminded us about this at every meeting by projecting the same slide.

📡 Watch Mode

bump --watch --bump patch

It sounds simple. It was the opposite of simple.

"Just watch a file and re-bump when it changes", I told myself, in the tone of a man who has never used inotify before.

Bro, I used inotify. Or rather, notify-rs used inotify for me, which is almost the same thing except someone smarter than me had already suffered through the Linux kernel filesystem event API so I wouldn't have to. God bless crate authors.

Watch mode works like this:

  1. You provide a --watch flag.
  2. bump registers a recursive file watcher on all files listed in your .bumpversion.toml.
  3. Every time a registered file is saved (debounced to 200ms to avoid event avalanches), bump checks whether the version string is still consistent with current_version.
  4. If it detects drift, it re-applies the bump.

This is either extremely useful for local development workflows or a deeply irresponsible footgun. We ship tools for adults. The lock safety is your problem.

# Watches VERSION, Cargo.toml, and README.md for changes, auto-bumps on save
bump --watch --bump patch --config-file .bumpversion.toml

# Oh no did I just? yes, yes you did. It already ran.
[watch] Detected change: Cargo.toml
[watch] Bumping patch: 0.2.1 → 0.2.2

🌐 Multi-Language Auto-Detection: --detect Is Doing God's Work

Previous bump2version was Rust-centric. You gave it files, it bumped files. Very obedient lil tool. Very rigid. Like a Rust compiler, actually.

The new --detect flag changes all that:

bump --bump minor --detect

This single command:

  1. Walks the entire directory tree (skipping target/, node_modules/, .git/, etc.)
  2. Finds every recognized manifest: Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, package.json, go.mod, pom.xml, build.gradle, Gemfile
  3. Checks each one for the current version string
  4. Rewrites every match in one coordinated pass

Six languages. One command.

cd my-monorepo
bump --current-version 0.1.0 --bump patch --detect --dry-run

# [detect][dry-run] Would update: Cargo.toml
# [detect][dry-run] Would update: pyproject.toml
# [detect][dry-run] Would update: package.json
# [detect][dry-run] Would update: pom.xml
# [detect][dry-run] Would update: go.mod
# [detect][dry-run] Would commit 5 file(s): 0.1.0 → 0.1.1

Full supported matrix:

Language Manifest Files
🦀 Rust Cargo.toml
🐍 Python pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, setup.py
🟨 JavaScript / Node.js package.json
🐹 Go go.mod
☕ Java pom.xml, build.gradle, build.gradle.kts
💎 Ruby Gemfile

The Go developers, in particular, messaged to say thank you. We thanked them for using Go despite everything.

🌍 Real Language Examples

Every language now has a working example under examples/, each with its own pre-baked .bumpversion.toml.

# Python project
bump --config-file examples/python/.bumpversion.toml --bump patch --dry-run
# [dry-run] Would commit 2 file(s): 0.1.0 → 0.1.1

# Node.js project
bump --config-file examples/nodejs/.bumpversion.toml --bump minor --dry-run
# [dry-run] Would commit 1 file(s): 0.1.0 → 0.2.0

# Java Maven project
bump --config-file examples/java/.bumpversion.toml --new-version 2.0.0 --dry-run
# [dry-run] Would commit 1 file(s): 0.1.0 → 2.0.0

# Ruby gemspec + Gemfile
bump --config-file examples/ruby/.bumpversion.toml --bump major --dry-run
# [dry-run] Would commit 2 file(s): 0.1.0 → 1.0.0

# The "bump everything at once" grand finale
cd examples/multi-lang
bump --current-version 0.1.0 --bump minor --detect --dry-run
# [detect][dry-run] Would update: Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, package.json, pom.xml, Gemfile, VERSION

6 ecosystems. 1 tool. Still forbids unsafe. We have standards.

🕸️ The Yew WASM App

You ever look at a perfectly good CLI tool and think: "This would be better if I could bump versions from a browser"?

No? Me neither. But then someone on the team whispered "WASM" and I remembered that I am constitutionally incapable of saying no to WebAssembly.

So now there is a Yew-based web application at examples/yew-app/. It:

  • Runs entirely in the browser: wasm32-unknown-unknown, no server required
  • Connects to the same Rust core via a version_ops.rs bridge module

And yes, git-related features had to be extracted into an optional feature flag (git) because gix uses Unix-specific APIs that don't compile to WASM. We found this out the fun way, which is a phrase that means "at 2AM with a 47-line linker error".

🤖 I Abused ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Again. More.

You may recall from my previous post that I abused Claude during 0.2.0 development. My lawyer said not to bring it up again.

So I won't bring up the fact that during 0.2.1 development, I made ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini:

  • Rewrite the detect.rs walk implementation 7 times until it correctly skipped node_modules without accidentally also skipping node_modules_backup (important distinction)
  • Argue with itself about whether SmallVec<[VersionPart; 8]> was better than SmallVec<[VersionPart; 4]> for typical semver usage (it is 8, empirically)

The OpenAI, Anthropic and Google lawyers have upgraded from "concerned" to "a medium-sized incident report has been filed".

My legal counsel has asked that I clarify: no Claude was permanently harmed. Tokens were consumed. Electricity was used. The --detect flag works correctly.

🚀 3 Binaries, One Package, Zero Confusing Changelog Entries

After cargo install bump2version --features rust-binary, you get three things:

Binary Use case

cargo-bump Cargo subcommand (cargo bump --bump patch)

The bump2version binary is not deprecated. It is not going anywhere. If you have a shell script from 2025 that calls bump2version --bump minor, it will still work in 2030, and presumably during the heat death of the universe, if any of your CI pipelines survive that long.

This was a deliberate choice. Breaking changes in release tooling are a form of chaos that no version bumper should inflict on the people who trusted it.

cargo bump --bump patch
bump2version --bump patch   # kept for backward compatibility

📋 The .bumpversion.toml Glow-Up

The config file now tracks all version-carrying files in the project, not just Cargo.toml:

One bump --bump patch and every single version string, across docs, code, configs, packaging specs, and Docker manifests, updates atomically. The Mossad agents reviewed this config and said "acceptable" which, from them, is essentially a standing ovation.

🦀 The Borrow Checker Tried to Ruin Watch Mode

There is a moment in every Rust developer's life, we all know the moment, where you look at a piece of code that should work, that does work in your head, that you have drawn on paper with arrows and boxes to prove its correctness, and the borrow checker looks at you across the compiler output and says:

error[E0505]: cannot move out of 'watcher' because it is borrowed

And then below that:

note: the borrow later used here

And then below that, a footnote that reads note: move occurs because... followed by a chain of reasoning so long it wraps around to the next terminal page.

The Yew WASM integration did this to me for different reasons: gix depends on Unix syscalls (openat, statx, platform symlink handling) that simply do not exist in wasm32-unknown-unknown. The linker error was 47 lines long and named three crates I had never heard of.

The fix: gating all git-related functionality behind a git feature flag that is disabled by default for WASM builds. Clean. Simple. The kind of solution that is obvious in retrospect and invisible before you spend four hours in the linker output.

The WASM app uses none of the git features. The CLI binary uses all of them. The feature graph is clean enough that my Mossad advisors called it "elegant" before immediately asking about the benchmark numbers.

This gets you bump, cargo-bump, and bump2version. All 3. No choices required. Just install and bump.

🚀 What Comes After 1,000,000×

Look, at some point the law of diminishing returns kicks in. We cannot make version bumping faster than the speed of light. (We checked. We asked the Mossad agents. They checked their slides. The answer was no.)

articles.title: Matching Blood Donors by GPS: The Geospatial Query Design Behind GeoBlood
articles.description: The naive version, and exactly how it fails     Every geospatial feature starts life like...
articles.body_html:
The naive version, and exactly how it fails

Every geospatial feature starts life like this:

`
js
// do not ship this
const donors = await Donor.find({ bloodType: 'B-', isAvailable: true });

const nearby = donors
  .map(d => ({ d, km: haversine(request.coords, d.coords) }))
  .filter(x => x.km <= 15)
  .sort((a, b) => a.km - b.km)
  .slice(0, 20);
`

It works. It works on your laptop with 300 seeded donors, and it works in staging, and it keeps working right up until the registry has real users in it. Then three things break at once.

It reads the whole collection. Every emergency request scans every matching donor document, ships them all into Node, and throws away 99% of them. Memory and CPU scale with total registry size, not with how many donors are actually nearby. That is exactly backwards from what you want.

It only asks for B negative. A B negative recipient can also receive from O negative. The naive query silently ignores an entire pool of the most valuable donors in the system. This is not a performance bug, it is a clinical one.

It sorts by distance and stops. The closest compatible donor might have given blood eleven days ago and be ineligible, or have ignored the last six alerts, or be O negative when an O negative donor two kilometres further out is the one you should be protecting for the trauma case that has not happened yet.

Fixing the first problem is a MongoDB index question. Fixing the second and third is a modelling question. You need both.

What 2dsphere actually does

Most developers use 2dsphere as a magic word. It is worth understanding what happens underneath, because the performance behaviour only makes sense once you do.

GeoJSON, and the coordinate order that bites everyone

First, store locations as GeoJSON, not as loose lat/lng fields:

js
const donorSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  bloodType:  { type: String, enum: ['O-','O+','A-','A+','B-','B+','AB-','AB+'], required: true },
  isAvailable:{ type: Boolean, default: true, index: true },
  verifiedAt: { type: Date },
  lastDonatedAt: { type: Date },

  // precise location. server side only, never projected to a client.
  location: {
    type:        { type: String, enum: ['Point'], required: true, default: 'Point' },
    coordinates: { type: [Number], required: true }   // [ longitude, latitude ]
  },

  // coarse location, safe to publish. see the privacy section.
  publicCell: { type: String, index: true }
});

We will add the geospatial index in a moment, and there is a reason it is not a plain { location: '2dsphere' } one. See the compound index section below, and the warning about having more than one.

[longitude, latitude]. Not lat, lng. GeoJSON follows the x, y convention from mathematics, while every mapping API, every phone SDK, and every human being says "latitude, longitude". If you get this backwards your queries will not error, they will just return the wrong people, and in Pakistan (roughly 31°N, 74°E) a flipped pair puts you in the Indian Ocean off Somalia. We caught ours in review. I would not bet on catching it in production, because a swapped-coordinate query still returns a plausible-looking empty result set, and an empty result set in this product reads as "no donors nearby" rather than "your query is broken."

Guard it at the boundary:

js
function toGeoPoint(lat, lng) {
  if (Math.abs(lat) > 90)  throw new Error(`latitude out of range: ${lat}`);
  if (Math.abs(lng) > 180) throw new Error(`longitude out of range: ${lng}`);
  return { type: 'Point', coordinates: [lng, lat] };
}

That Math.abs(lat) > 90 check catches the swap for most of the inhabited world for free, because valid longitudes routinely exceed 90 and valid latitudes never do.

2d versus 2dsphere
MongoDB has two geospatial index types and they are not interchangeable.

2d is the legacy index. It treats coordinates as points on a flat plane. That is fine for a game map or a floor plan. It is wrong for a country, and badly wrong once your users span more than one, because a degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and about 85 km in Lahore and about 0 km at the pole. Distances computed on a flat plane get progressively more wrong as you move away from the equator, and any radius search near the antimeridian or the poles breaks outright.

2dsphere models the Earth as a sphere. Distances come back in metres, radius searches are true great-circle searches, and geometry that crosses the antimeridian behaves. For anything involving real people in real places, use 2dsphere. There is no interesting tradeoff here.

How a circle becomes a B-tree range
MongoDB's 2dsphere index is built on Google's S2 library. The trick S2 pulls is this: project the sphere onto the six faces of a circumscribed cube, recursively subdivide each face into a quadtree, and number the resulting cells along a Hilbert curve. Because the Hilbert curve preserves locality, cells that are near each other on the sphere get numbers that are near each other on the number line. A two-dimensional problem becomes a one-dimensional one, and one dimension is exactly what a B-tree is good at.

So when you ask for "everyone within 15 km of this point", MongoDB does not compute 15 km against every document. It computes a covering: a small set of S2 cells whose union contains your query circle. Each cell is a contiguous range of integers. Each range is a contiguous B-tree scan. Then it re-checks the candidates that came back, because the covering is a superset of the circle and includes some slop at the edges.

The left panel is what a fixed grid would give you: every cell the same size, so you scan a lot of cells that are almost entirely outside the circle. The right panel is what S2 does. Large cells in the interior where a single range covers a lot of ground, small cells only at the boundary where precision matters. Fewer ranges, less slop, and the index does the geometry instead of your application server.

Two practical consequences fall out of this:

2dsphere indexes are large. Every document contributes multiple cell entries, not one. Budget for it. On a nonprofit's database, index size is a real line item.
Building one on a populated collection is not free. If you learned MongoDB before 4.2 your instinct here is { background: true }. Do not reach for it: background index builds were deprecated in 4.2 and the option was removed in 4.4. Since 4.2 there is a single optimized build that takes an exclusive lock only at the start and end and yields in between, so the old foreground/background choice no longer exists. Plan the build window anyway, because "yields to readers" is not the same as "free" when your users may be mid-emergency.

2dsphere indexes are also sparse by default, and they ignore an explicit sparse option. A donor document with no location simply is not in the index, which is the behaviour you want and also a good reason to make the field required.

$near, $geoWithin, $geoNear: three ways to ask, three different bills

This is the part I see people get wrong most often, including me, for about a month.


$near and $nearSphere
js
db.donors.find({
  location: {
    $nearSphere: {
      $geometry: { type: 'Point', coordinates: [74.3587, 31.5204] },
      $maxDistance: 15000   // metres
    }
  }
});

Returns documents sorted by distance, nearest first, always. That sounds like a gift and it is actually a constraint. You are allowed to add your own sort(), but the docs are blunt about what happens: MongoDB performs a second sort operation, re-ordering documents it has already ordered, and on a large collection that costs you. So if your ranking is anything other than pure distance, $near is not free, it is a sort you are paying for and then throwing away. The docs even point you at the alternative: if you do not need the ordering, use $geoWithin, which returns unsorted results.

$nearSphere with GeoJSON and $near with GeoJSON behave the same on a 2dsphere index; the distinction only matters for legacy coordinate pairs, where $near measures in radians on a flat plane and $nearSphere measures on the sphere. Use GeoJSON and the ambiguity disappears.


### geoWithin with $centerSphere
js
db.donors.find({
  location: {
    $geoWithin: {
      $centerSphere: [[74.3587, 31.5204], 15 / 6378.1]   // radius in radians
    }
  },
  bloodType: { $in: ['B-', 'O-'] },
  isAvailable: true
});

Pure membership test. No sorting, no distance in the output, and that is why it is the cheapest of the three. $centerSphere takes its radius in radians, so you divide your kilometres by the Earth's radius (6378.1 km). Yes, this is an odd API. Write the helper once:

js
const kmToRadians = km => km / 6378.1;

$geoWithin is the right choice when you genuinely do not need ordering: counting eligible donors in a city for the partnerships dashboard, checking whether a request has any viable pool at all before you spend a notification budget on it, warming a cache.

$geoNear in the aggregation pipeline 

js
{
  $geoNear: {
    near: { type: 'Point', coordinates: [74.3587, 31.5204] },
    distanceField: 'distanceMeters',
    minDistance: 5000,
    maxDistance: 15000,
    query: { bloodType: { $in: ['B-', 'O-'] }, isAvailable: true },
    spherical: true
  }
}

This is what we actually run. $geoNear gives you three things the others do not:

distanceField writes the computed distance into each document, so you can use it in later stages rather than recomputing it in Node.
minDistance and maxDistance together describe an annulus, a ring with a hole in the middle. That is the whole basis of staged expansion, below. For GeoJSON points both are in metres; for legacy coordinate pairs they are in radians, which is one more reason to standardise on GeoJSON.
The query sub-document belongs to the stage, not to a later $match. This matters more than it looks.

$geoNear has two hard rules. It must be the first stage in the pipeline, so if you need to pre-filter, the filter goes inside query (with one exception: you cannot put a $near predicate in there). And it requires a geospatial index, which leads directly to the trap in the next section.

And here is the trap that cost me an afternoon. This looks equivalent:

js
// slow: geoNear returns nearest documents, THEN they get filtered
[
  { $geoNear: { near: pt, distanceField: 'd', maxDistance: 15000, spherical: true } },
  { $match: { bloodType: { $in: ['B-', 'O-'] } } },
  { $limit: 20 }
]

It is not. $geoNear walks outward from the centre and emits documents in distance order. With the filter in a separate $match, it emits every donor in the radius and the pipeline throws most of them away afterwards. In a city where B negative and O negative together are maybe 10% of the registry, you are materialising ten times more documents than you need, and the $limit at the end saves you nothing because the work already happened. Move the predicate into query and the stage has a chance to stop early. Same result, far fewer documents examined.

I am deliberately describing the observable behaviour rather than the internals, because the docs do not commit to how query is evaluated and I do not want to put words in their mouth. Measure it on your own data instead of trusting either of us:

js
db.donors.aggregate(pipeline).explain('executionStats');
// compare totalDocsExamined against nReturned.
// if that ratio is much above 1, your predicate is in the wrong place.

That ratio is the number I would put on a dashboard if I could only keep one.

The compound index, and the trap that comes with it

js
db.donors.createIndex(
  { bloodType: 1, isAvailable: 1, location: '2dsphere' },
  { name: 'match_by_type_avail_geo' }
);

Do not also keep a plain { location: '2dsphere' } index alongside this one. This is the mistake I want to save you: if a collection has more than one 2d index or more than one 2dsphere index, $geoNear errors out unless you tell it which to use via the key option. It is a startlingly easy state to reach, because the natural thing to do is add the simple geo index first, get it working, then add a compound one later and never remove the original. Either drop the redundant index or be explicit:

js
{ $geoNear: { /* ... */ key: 'location' } }

On field order I want to be careful. The common advice, which I followed, is to put the equality fields ahead of the geo field so the index prefix narrows the candidate set before any spherical geometry happens. It matched what I measured on our data. But MongoDB's documentation does not actually publish guidance on ordering within a compound 2dsphere index, so treat this as an empirical result from one registry and not as a rule. Build it both ways, run explain, keep the winner.

Worth knowing about compound indexes generally: up to 32 fields, at most one hashed field (they are not forbidden, which is what I would have guessed), and a compound index that includes a geospatial field only indexes documents that actually have a value in that geo field.

Compatibility is a matrix, not an equality check

Here is where the domain stops being a generic proximity search.

ABO/Rh compatibility is directional. An O negative donor can give to any of the eight recipient types. An AB positive donor can give only to AB positive. Nobody's intuition gets this right the first time, and the direction is easy to flip because "AB positive is the universal recipient" and "O negative is the universal donor" are two halves of the same fact pointing opposite ways.


Read the grid rows as donors and columns as recipients. The staircase shape is the whole point: the pool of people who can help you is a set, not a value. We publish the same thing for non-engineers as a blood group compatibility chart, which is a decent sanity check if you are encoding this yourself.

Encode it once, in one place, and never let anyone write bloodType: request.bloodType again:

js
// COMPATIBLE_DONORS[recipientType] = donor types that can give to them
const COMPATIBLE_DONORS = Object.freeze({
  'O-':  ['O-'],
  'O+':  ['O-', 'O+'],
  'A-':  ['O-', 'A-'],
  'A+':  ['O-', 'O+', 'A-', 'A+'],
  'B-':  ['O-', 'B-'],
  'B+':  ['O-', 'O+', 'B-', 'B+'],
  'AB-': ['O-', 'A-', 'B-', 'AB-'],
  'AB+': ['O-', 'O+', 'A-', 'A+', 'B-', 'B+', 'AB-', 'AB+']
});

Two things happen the moment you ship this.

The viable pool widens, sometimes dramatically. A B negative request goes from one matching type to two, and one of those two is the most flexible type in the registry. An AB positive request goes from one type to all eight. In a thin market, which is what every new city is, this is the difference between a match and a dead request.

You immediately create a new problem. If every request happily recruits O negative donors, and O negative is roughly 5% of most populations, then your universal donors get hammered with alerts for requests that four other types could have covered. They burn out, they mute notifications, and they are unavailable for the O negative recipient who has no alternative at all. The most valuable resource in the system is the one your naive ranking spends first.

So compatibility widens the pool, and then ranking has to protect it.

Worth knowing that not all demand is one-off either. Someone in an accident needs blood once. Someone with thalassemia major needs a transfusion every two to five weeks, for life, and Pakistan has one of the highest carrier rates in the world. Emergency demand wants maximum reach right now. Recurring demand wants a small stable set of donors who come back. Broadcasting to both the same way optimises for neither.

Ranking: distance is one term, not the answer

Once the candidate set is right, the question becomes who to actually wake up. We score, then sort, and distance is only the first input.


js
const pipeline = [
  {
    $geoNear: {
      near: { type: 'Point', coordinates: [lng, lat] },
      distanceField: 'distanceMeters',
      minDistance: wave.minMeters,
      maxDistance: wave.maxMeters,
      query: {
        bloodType:   { $in: COMPATIBLE_DONORS[request.bloodType] },
        isAvailable: true,
        verifiedAt:  { $ne: null },
        lastDonatedAt: { $lt: cooldownCutoff }   // eligibility window
      },
      spherical: true
    }
  },
  {
    $addFields: {
      // lower is better, all terms normalised to roughly the same range
      score: {
        $add: [
          { $divide: ['$distanceMeters', 1000] },                    // km
          { $multiply: [{ $ifNull: ['$rarityPenalty', 0] }, 4] },    // protect scarce types
          { $multiply: [{ $subtract: [1, { $ifNull: ['$responseRate', 0.5] }] }, 6] },
          { $cond: [{ $eq: ['$isOnline', true] }, -3, 0] }           // reachable right now
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  { $sort:  { score: 1 } },
  { $limit: wave.notifyBudget },
  { $project: { location: 0 } }   // never leaves the server
];

The terms, and why each one is there:

Distance in km. The base. One point of score per kilometre gives every other term a natural unit to be calibrated against, which matters far more than the exact weights.

Rarity penalty. Set higher for O negative than for O positive. A weight of 4 means an O negative donor has to be roughly four kilometres closer than an O positive donor to be picked ahead of them for a request that either could serve. For an O negative recipient, where there is no alternative, the penalty is zero. This is the cheapest possible model of a scarce resource and it has held up.

Inverse response rate. A donor who has answered 8 of their last 10 alerts is worth more than an equally close donor who has answered 0 of 10. The default for a new donor is 0.5, deliberately optimistic, so newcomers get a chance to establish a record instead of being locked out by a cold start.

Online bonus. Someone with the app in the foreground can respond in seconds. Worth about three kilometres.

The eligibility filter is a filter, not a term. Someone who donated nine days ago is not a worse match, they are not a match. Clinical rules belong in query where they cannot be outweighed by a good score somewhere else. This is a principle worth being rigid about: anything that could harm a person is a hard predicate, anything that is merely a preference is a score term.

Two engineering notes on the pipeline itself. Everything after $geoNear runs in memory, so the query sub-document is doing the heavy lifting and the scoring stages should never see a large input. And $project: { location: 0 } is not decoration. The precise coordinates are the most sensitive field in the collection and they should be structurally incapable of reaching a response body.

Radius expansion: what to do when nobody is there

The obvious response to "no donors found in 15 km" is to search 200 km instead. Do not just widen the radius. Widen it in waves, and time the waves.


js
const WAVES = [
  { minKm: 0,  maxKm: 5,   delayMs: 0,       notifyBudget: 25 },
  { minKm: 5,  maxKm: 15,  delayMs: 90_000,  notifyBudget: 60 },
  { minKm: 15, maxKm: 50,  delayMs: 300_000, notifyBudget: 150 },
  { minKm: 50, maxKm: 200, delayMs: 900_000, notifyBudget: 400 }
];

Notice minKm. Each wave queries an annulus, not a disc, which is what minDistance on $geoNear is for. Wave 3 does not re-notify everyone wave 2 already reached. Without that, a four-stage expansion sends the closest donor four push notifications for the same request, and there is no faster way to teach someone to disable your notifications.

The reasons for staging rather than one wide search:

Alert fatigue is the real scarce resource. A donor's willingness to open your notification is finite and it does not recover quickly. Every alert sent to someone 180 km away who was never going to travel is a withdrawal from that account. Push notification delivery costs almost nothing, so the temptation is to blast, and the temptation is wrong. The budget that matters is attention.

Distance correlates with response probability, non-linearly. Someone 3 km away might come. Someone 40 km away might come for a family member or a rare type. Someone 180 km away is realistically only relevant for a rare type with a long lead time. The waves encode that.

The clinical window sets the clock, not the other way round. The delays exist because a donor needs time to see, decide, and reply. Ninety seconds is roughly the floor for that. If you escalate faster than people can answer, you are not searching harder, you are just spamming in sequence.

The escalation loop is straightforward and should be idempotent, because it will be retried:

js
async function runWave(requestId, waveIndex) {
  const request = await BloodRequest.findById(requestId);
  if (!request || request.status !== 'open') return;   // fulfilled or cancelled

  const wave = WAVES[waveIndex];
  if (!wave) return markUnfulfilled(request);

  const matches = await Donor.aggregate(buildPipeline(request, wave));
  await notify(matches, request);

  await BloodRequest.updateOne(
    { _id: requestId },
    { $set: { lastWave: waveIndex }, $inc: { notifiedCount: matches.length } }
  );

  const next = WAVES[waveIndex + 1];
  if (next) scheduleWave(requestId, waveIndex + 1, next.delayMs);
}

Staged expansion also hands you the most useful growth signal you will get. When the donor pool for a city like Lahore consistently exhausts wave two before finding a match, that is not a matching problem. That is a recruitment problem with a postcode attached, and no amount of query tuning fixes it.

The status !== 'open' check at the top is the most important line in it. Requests get fulfilled between waves, and a system that keeps escalating after a match has been found is worse than one that never escalated at all.

The privacy tradeoff: match on the precise point, publish something else
This is the design decision I am most confident about and it is the one that constrains everything else.

A blood donor registry is, structurally, a database of people who have told you their health details and where they sleep. If you render donor pins on a public map at their true coordinates, you have built a tool for finding a stranger's home that happens to also match blood donors. There is no acceptable version of that, and "we only show approximate pins" is not a fix if the approximation is naive.

The architecture we settled on separates two fields with two completely different lifecycles:

location is the precise GeoJSON point. It is indexed, it is used for matching, it is never projected into any API response, and it is stripped in the pipeline rather than in a serialiser, because serialisers get bypassed and pipelines do not.

publicCell is a coarse, deterministic, stable cell identifier. It is what the map renders.


The word doing the work there is deterministic. The intuitive approach is to add random jitter to the coordinates before publishing them, a few hundred metres in a random direction. It feels private and it is not, because the jitter is re-rolled on every request. Poll the endpoint forty times, average the results, and the noise cancels out to reveal the true point. That is the left panel. It is a two-line attack against a defence that looks reasonable.

A stable coarse cell has no such weakness. Poll it a million times and you get the same cell, because it is a pure function of the donor's location, not of the request:

js
const ngeohash = require('ngeohash');

// precision 6 is roughly 1.2 km x 0.6 km. tune per market density.
function toPublicCell(lat, lng) {
  return ngeohash.encode(lat, lng, 6);
}

function cellCentroid(cell) {
  const { latitude, longitude } = ngeohash.decode(cell);
  return [longitude, latitude];   // GeoJSON order
}

The map draws the centroid of the cell, identically for every donor inside it. Geohash has a well-known edge case (neighbouring points can sit in different cells if they straddle a boundary) but for this purpose that is harmless: it produces an occasional pin that is a cell away from where you would expect, and never a pin that is more precise than intended.

Three more rules that fall out of the same reasoning:

Bucket the distances too. Returning distanceMeters: 2847 from three different requesters is trilateration with extra steps. Three circles and you have the intersection. Round to something coarse before it leaves the server:

js
const publicDistance = km =>
  km < 1  ? 'under 1 km'
: km < 5  ? `${Math.round(km)} km away`
:           `${Math.round(km / 5) * 5} km away`;

Pseudonymous identity until both sides consent. The public map shows a handle and a blood type, Bpos#9EDA · B+, not a name and not a photo. The request/accept handshake gates everything else. Chat opens only after acceptance, and no phone number is ever exposed, which is the single most common failure mode of the WhatsApp-group approach this product replaces.

Meeting points are institutions, not addresses. Coordination happens at the hospital or the blood bank. The product never needs to route two strangers to each other's homes, so it never offers to.

The honest cost of all this: matching is slightly less precise, the map is slightly less satisfying to look at, and you cannot show a donor exactly how far away they are. I will take all three. The failure mode on the other side of that tradeoff is not a degraded feature, it is someone getting hurt, and a nonprofit that harms its donors has no second chance at recruiting them.

What I would tell myself at the start

Put the domain rule in the index, not in the application. The compatibility set inside $geoNear's query is the single highest-leverage line in the system. Everything I got wrong early was a version of doing domain filtering after the database had already done the expensive part.

explain('executionStats') before you optimise anything. The ratio of totalDocsExamined to nReturned told me more in five minutes than a week of guessing. If it is not close to 1, a predicate is in the wrong place.

Model the scarce resource explicitly. Not distance, not latency: donor attention, and O negative supply. Both are exhaustible, neither shows up in any performance metric, and a system that spends them freely looks perfectly healthy on a dashboard right up until nobody answers.

Decide the privacy architecture before you write the first query. Retrofitting coarse locations onto a system that already ships precise ones means auditing every response body you have ever written. Starting with two fields and a pipeline that strips one of them costs nothing on day one.

Anything clinical is a filter, never a weight. Eligibility windows, verification status, compatibility. The moment one of those becomes a score term, a sufficiently good score somewhere else can override it, and in this domain that is not a ranking bug.

The index rebuild, incidentally, is still not finished the way I want it. That is a different article, and a more embarrassing one.

GeoBlood is free, nonprofit, and volunteer built. If you want to look at the product side of it: geoblood.org, App Store, Google Play.

If you are running the other half of this problem and want to compare notes on donor verification, alert fatigue or location privacy, the comments are open.

I write about backend architecture, iOS, and infrastructure at obaidaqeel.com.

articles.title: Wrapping redirect() in a try/catch in Next.js Can Silently Swallow the Redirect
articles.description: This one catches people specifically because the code looks like careful error handling, and it's...
articles.body_html:
This one catches people specifically because the code looks like careful error handling, and it's actually the thing breaking the exact feature it's wrapped around.

The Setup That Looks Like Responsible Error Handling 

// actions/auth.ts
'use server';

export async function login(formData: FormData) {
  try {
    const email = formData.get('email') as string;
    const password = formData.get('password') as string;

    const user = await verifyCredentials(email, password);
    if (!user) {
      return { error: 'Invalid credentials' };
    }

    await setSessionCookie(user);
    redirect('/dashboard');
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Login failed:', error);
    return { error: 'Something went wrong' };
  }
}

This looks like exactly the kind of defensive coding you'd want, wrap the risky operations, catch anything unexpected, return a clean error instead of crashing. It also means a successful login never actually redirects anywhere, and the console gets a confusing, misleading error log every single time someone logs in correctly.

Why This Happens

redirect() in Next.js doesn't work like a normal function returning a value that tells the framework "please navigate now." It works by throwing a special internal error, effectively an escape hatch, that Next.js's own machinery catches at a higher level in the rendering or request lifecycle, and uses to actually trigger the navigation. This is genuinely how the feature is implemented under the hood, not a bug, it's a deliberate mechanism for interrupting normal execution flow to redirect.

A try/catch block doesn't know or care that this particular thrown error is special. It catches everything thrown within its boundary, indiscriminately, which includes this internal redirect signal exactly the same way it would catch a genuine database error or a network failure. Your catch block intercepts it, logs a confusing "Login failed" message for what was actually a completely successful login, and returns your generic error response instead of ever letting the redirect signal propagate up to where Next.js needs to see it.

Why the Console Log Makes This Extra Confusing

The logged error typically has a distinctive-looking message or code related to Next.js's internal redirect mechanism, not a normal JavaScript error you'd immediately recognize. Someone unfamiliar with this specific gotcha sees an unfamiliar-looking error logged on every successful login and reasonably assumes something is actually broken, when the "error" being caught is, ironically, the successful outcome trying to happen.

The Actual Fix: Call redirect() Outside the try/catch 

// actions/auth.ts
'use server';

export async function login(formData: FormData) {
  const email = formData.get('email') as string;
  const password = formData.get('password') as string;

  let user;
  try {
    user = await verifyCredentials(email, password);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Login failed:', error);
    return { error: 'Something went wrong' };
  }

  if (!user) {
    return { error: 'Invalid credentials' };
  }

  await setSessionCookie(user);
  redirect('/dashboard'); // outside any try/catch, free to throw its internal signal cleanly
}

Scoping the try/catch specifically around the operation that can genuinely fail in an unexpected way, the credential verification, database call, whatever's actually risky, and calling redirect() afterward, outside that block entirely, means its internal throw mechanism reaches Next.js cleanly, without your own error handling accidentally standing in the way.

If You Need Try/Catch Around Code That Includes a redirect() Call

Sometimes the structure genuinely requires a broader try block. In that case, explicitly re-throw anything that looks like a Next.js redirect or notFound signal, rather than treating everything caught as a genuine error:

import { isRedirectError } from 'next/dist/client/components/redirect';

try {
  // some code that includes a redirect() call somewhere within it
} catch (error) {
  if (isRedirectError(error)) {
    throw error; // let it propagate, this isn't a real error
  }
  console.error('Actual error:', error);
  return { error: 'Something went wrong' };
}

This pattern is more defensive but also more fragile, since it depends on an internal Next.js utility rather than a fully public, stable API. Restructuring the code to keep redirect() outside any try/catch entirely, the first fix above, is the cleaner, more robust solution whenever the code can reasonably be organized that way.

Where Else This Bites

The exact same issue applies to notFound(), which uses the same underlying throw-based mechanism. Any Server Action, Server Component, or route handler with a broad try/catch wrapping code that also calls redirect() or notFound() anywhere within that boundary is at risk of this exact silent failure, not just login flows specifically.

The Actual Rule

Never let a try/catch block unintentionally wrap a call to redirect() or notFound(). Scope error handling tightly around the specific operations that can genuinely throw a real error, and keep redirect and not-found calls outside that boundary, or explicitly detect and re-throw them if the structure genuinely requires a broader catch.

If you've got a Server Action with a broad try/catch that also calls redirect() somewhere inside it, go check whether that redirect is actually firing, or silently getting logged as a mysterious error instead. Drop what you find in the comments.

articles.body_html:
7 Node.js Mistakes That Are Quietly Killing Your Backend

Your API works. It passes the demo. Then it hits real traffic — and everything slows to a crawl, memory balloons, and one bad request takes the whole thing down.

Most of the time it's not a hard bug. It's one of these seven quiet mistakes almost every backend developer makes early on. Fix them and your Node.js backend gets faster, safer, and far harder to knock over.

1. Blocking the event loop

Node is single-threaded for your code. One synchronous, heavy operation freezes every request, not just the current one.

// ❌ blocks everyone while it runs
const hash = crypto.pbkdf2Sync(password, salt, 100000, 64, 'sha512')

// ✅ async version keeps the loop free
crypto.pbkdf2(password, salt, 100000, 64, 'sha512', (err, hash) => { /* ... */ })

Rule of thumb: if a function ends in Sync, ask what it's blocking. JSON.parse on a huge payload, big loops, synchronous file reads — same danger.

2. Not handling promise rejections

An unhandled rejection can crash the whole process in modern Node.

// ❌ if this throws, nothing catches it
app.get('/user', async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.findUser(req.query.id)
  res.json(user)
})

// ✅ wrap async handlers so errors reach your error middleware
const wrap = fn => (req, res, next) => Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next)
app.get('/user', wrap(async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.findUser(req.query.id)
  res.json(user)
}))

3. No database indexes

Your query is fast on 100 rows and dies on 100,000. Without an index, the database scans every single document.

If a query filters or sorts on a field, that field almost always needs an index. One line often turns a 900ms query into a 3ms one. Check your slow queries before users find them for you.

4. Trusting user input

Every value from the client is hostile until proven otherwise. Unvalidated input is how you get injection, crashes, and garbage in your database.

Validate the shape and type of every request body and query param at the edge (a schema validator makes this one line per route). Never build a database query by string-concatenating user input.

5. Leaking secrets and stack traces

Two classics: committing a .env file, and sending raw error objects to the client.

// ❌ hands attackers your stack trace, file paths, and query internals
res.status(500).json({ error: err })

// ✅ log the detail, return something safe
console.error(err)          // or your error tracker
res.status(500).json({ message: 'Something went wrong' })

Keep secrets in environment variables, never in the repo. Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.

6. No timeouts on outbound calls

Calling another API or service with no timeout means one slow dependency can hang your requests forever and pile up until you run out of connections.

Always set a timeout on outbound HTTP calls and database operations. Fail fast, return a clear error, and your backend stays responsive even when something downstream is having a bad day.

7. Console.log as your only observability

console.log is fine for local dev. In production it tells you nothing when a real user hits a bug at 2 AM and you're asleep.

Use structured logging and an error tracker that alerts you the moment something breaks — with the stack trace and the request that caused it. The goal: you find the bug before your users report it.

The pattern behind all seven

Every one of these is the same lesson: code that works in a demo is not code that survives production. The gap between "it runs" and "it holds up under real load, real users, and real attackers" is exactly what separates a hobby project from a hireable backend developer.

None of this is advanced. It's just rarely taught in order — which is why so many devs learn it the painful way, in production.

I run AS Backend Institute, where we teach backend and full-stack development the way it actually works in production — not just tutorials that stop at "hello world." If you want a structured path, start here.

If this saved you one 2 AM incident, share it with a developer who's still doing console.log in production. 🙂

articles.body_html:
Start dragging, push past the bottom of the window, and the page scrolls along with you. Let go, and you get a single PNG of a region that was never on screen all at once.

The extension I relied on went away

For a long time, GoFullPage was just part of the furniture. Two jobs, mostly:

  • Screenshotting server maintenance logs for my records (logs are tall)
  • Capturing a whole page to send to a client

Then one day it stopped working for me. I never dug into exactly what happened — only that something quietly useful wasn't there anymore, with no way to know if it was coming back.

The logs, meanwhile, kept being tall. The clients kept needing pages.

So: fine. I'll build one.

From here to there

It's called Koko Soko (ココソコ). Koko is "here" in Japanese and soko is "there" — you point at one, then the other, and it takes everything in between.

  • Click the toolbar icon and choose Select Area
  • Drag out the region you want
  • It scrolls through your selection, captures it in tiles, and stitches the tiles into one PNG

The auto-scroll at the edges is the entire reason I built this instead of reaching for another full-page tool. You can select a region far larger than one screenful. Capturing and stitching both happen inside the browser; no image is sent anywhere.

There's a Full Page mode too — top to bottom, the thing I'd been using GoFullPage for.

  • Chrome Web Store:

    ココソコ - Koko Soko - Chrome Web Store

    ココからソコまで、範囲を指定してスクロールごとスクショ / Capture anything from here to there — select a range and shoot the whole scroll.

    chromewebstore.google.com

How it's put together

TypeScript throughout, in three folders:

  • src/background.ts — the service worker. Calls chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab, throttles it, retries it. Nothing else.
  • src/content/ — the selection overlay, coordinate math, tiled capture, canvas stitching, hiding fixed elements while shooting
  • src/shared/ — utilities shared between background and popup

The only permissions are activeTab and scripting. No standing read/write access to every site you visit.

One build note that's easy to miss: Vite transpiles, it doesn't type-check. A green build tells you nothing about your types. So tsconfig.json sets "noEmit": true and type checking lives in its own script (tsc --noEmit) that I run before committing.

Two things along the way made me stop and go "ah, that's why."

The box that flew away

The first version had a great bug: scroll while you're dragging, and the selection box shoots off across the page.

I was storing the mouse event's coordinates as-is.

// nope
let start = { x: event.clientX, y: event.clientY };

clientX / clientY answer the question "where is this on screen right now" — origin at the top-left of the viewport. Which means they quietly change meaning the instant you scroll. Click 100px from the top, scroll down 200px, and "100px from the top of the screen" now points at a completely different paragraph.

What I actually needed was the position within the document — anchored to the top of the page, unmoved by scrolling. The conversion is just the scroll offset:

// where it appears on screen -> where it lives in the document
toContent(clientX: number, clientY: number): Point {
  return { x: clientX + scrollX, y: clientY + scrollY }
}

// where it lives in the document -> where it appears on screen
toClient(x: number, y: number): Point {
  return { x: x - scrollX, y: y - scrollY }
}

And then one rule, which is really the whole fix: store the selection in content coordinates, convert to client coordinates only at paint time.

function render(): void {
  if (state.kind !== "selecting") return;

  const startClient = state.target.toClient(state.start.x, state.start.y);
  const currentClient = state.target.toClient(state.current.x, state.current.y);

  overlay.setRect({
    top: Math.min(startClient.y, currentClient.y),
    left: Math.min(startClient.x, currentClient.x),
    width: Math.abs(startClient.x - currentClient.x),
    height: Math.abs(startClient.y - currentClient.y),
  });
}

(The Math.min / Math.abs pair is what stops a bottom-right-to-top-left drag from producing a rectangle with negative width.)

That early return is quietly doing double duty. State is a discriminated union — { kind: "idle" } | { kind: "selecting"; start: Point; ... } | { kind: "capturing" } — so once you've bailed out on everything that isn't selecting, TypeScript lets you read state.start. With one flat type full of optional fields, reading selection coordinates mid-capture would have been a runtime bug instead of a red squiggle.

The second click

This one took me the longest.

Koko Soko runs on activeTab, injecting its content script at the moment you click the icon:

chrome.scripting.executeScript({
  target: { tabId }, // which tab
  files: ["content.js"], // what to run
});

That's how you avoid ever holding "read and change everything on every site you visit" — better for store review, and better for the permission dialog people actually read.

And then the second click on the same tab turned the console red.

Uncaught SyntaxError: Identifier 'WindowScrollTarget' has already been declared

What was actually going on

A content script runs in what Chrome calls an isolated world:

An isolated world is a private execution environment that isn't accessible to the page or other extensions.

Private from the page, sure. Not private from me, sixty seconds ago:

  • First injection → class WindowScrollTarget declared at the top level of that world
  • Second injection → same declaration, same scope
  • Collision

A normal page wipes its scope clean on reload. Injection doesn't reload anything, so the first run's leftovers are still sitting there when the second run walks in.

Worth noticing that this is a SyntaxError, not a runtime error. The engine parses the whole file before running a line of it, spots the duplicate name, and throws the file out. You can't try/catch your way out of that — the catch block is inside the file that never ran. Which is why the fix ended up in the build config rather than the code.

Fix one: an IIFE

Emit the content script — and only the content script — as an IIFE.

// vite.content.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    rollupOptions: {
      input: { content: resolve(__dirname, "src/content/index.ts") },
      output: {
        entryFileNames: "[name].js",
        format: "iife", // <- this
      },
    },
    outDir: "dist",
    emptyOutDir: false, // don't wipe the background/popup output
  },
});

The bundle comes out wrapped:

(function () {
  "use strict";
  class WindowScrollTarget {
    /* ... */
  }
})();

A function that runs itself the moment it's defined. Everything declared inside exists only inside. Inject it ten times and you get ten separate scopes that have never met each other, and nothing at all lands in the global one. background.ts and popup.ts stay ordinary ES modules.

Fix two: a flag on window

The IIFE stops the collision, but not the execution. Ten scopes means ten passes through the same initialization — ten sets of event listeners hanging off one shared DOM, and one drag firing every one of them.

So I left a marker:

if (!window.__kokosoko__) {
  window.__kokosoko__ = true;

  // everything below runs on the first injection only
  let state: State = { kind: "idle" };
  const overlay = createOverlay();
  // ...register listeners
}

It's tempting to say this works because window is shared. It isn't — the isolated world gets its own window, and window.__kokosoko__ is invisible to the page's own JavaScript.

It works because window outlives the injection. The IIFE scope is built from scratch on every click and remembers nothing; the world's window stays put until you navigate away. Longevity is the only property being used here.

(TypeScript will object that Window has no such member, which declare global and interface declaration merging settle in about four lines.)

So: the IIFE prevents name collisions, the flag prevents duplicate side effects. Two problems wearing one costume.

The seam I left open

Slack, Notion and friends scroll a container rather than the page itself. Koko Soko doesn't handle those yet — the whole thing is built around window.scrollTo().

It is, however, built around it behind an interface:

export interface ScrollTarget {
  getScroll(): Point;
  scrollTo(y: number): void;
  getMaxScrollY(): number;
  getWindowRect(): Rect;
  toContent(clientX: number, clientY: number): Point;
  toClient(x: number, y: number): Point;
  scrollToShowContentAt(y: number): void;
}

There's exactly one implementation today (WindowScrollTarget). Adding an ElementScrollTarget should leave the capture loop and the coordinate math untouched. Premature abstraction is a genuine sin, but when you already know the second implementation is coming, leaving the seam open is just reading ahead.

Wrapping up

This started with something I depended on disappearing, which is an irritating way to start anything. It ended with coordinate systems, a SyntaxError I'd never seen in my life, and a build setting that turned out to be the fix for a bug I'd been trying to solve in code.

If the selection overlay felt suspiciously smooth to write, that's because I'd already built one for ShoText, an extension that OCRs a region of the screen onto your clipboard. Half of this project was me quietly copying myself.
